title: Sequoia's Former Boss on Reading People: What Happens Before 14 Sets Your Core
dek: Digging into his own refugee family's history, he found that the imprint you unconsciously absorb from your parents before you're 12, 13, 14 stays with you for life; what changes afterward is the external intensity, not the core.
why: Not an investing lesson but a retrospective on origins, reading people, and writing. The second half on venture capital's structural shifts and the great man theory is the most valuable; the family history up front is more personal.
who: Founders, early-stage investors, and angels: for anyone who wants to know which of 40 years of people-picking experience still applies and which has expired.
skip: The discussion of current affairs and antisemitism starting at 11 minutes is more of a personal stance and can be fast-forwarded.

points.h: The grandfather who waited for the situation to pass disappeared
points.body: Moritz's two grandfathers were two responses to the same catastrophe. His maternal grandfather was a lower-court judge in Bavaria, had fought at Verdun in World War I, believed in the durability of the state, and had a pension he was unwilling to give up, so he delayed leaving and was eventually sent east with his wife and vanished from history. The other grandfather was nearly blind, supported his family alone by trading cattle, had no pension to wait for, and left with his wife 72 hours before the war broke out—three days later and they too would have died. Moritz says the lesson is not a moral judgment but that you must always have a bolt hole to hide in, and never too many passports.

points.h: His most effective question makes people cry on the spot
points.body: When he interviews people, he always asks one question: looking back, if there was one thing, one action you could have done differently, what would it be. He remembers a person interviewing at Sequoia bursting into tears when asked this—the man was the son of a Latino immigrant, had stolen candy from a corner grocery store with friends around age 12, the owner told his father, and his father dragged him back by the ear, made him apologize and empty his pockets. Years later, asked this question, the first thing he thought of was still the shame brought to his family. Moritz says many people conducting interviews aren't really listening to the answers.

points.h: He sorted everyone he knew on Zoom
points.body: Inspired by a TV series about a French village in World War II, he divided people into three categories: resisters, the silent, and collaborators. During the pandemic, in those Zoom meetings with a dozen little windows, he would stare at each person he knew and think: if these people lived in a French village in the 1940s, who would stay silent, who would resist, who would collaborate. He says resisters are always a tiny minority, because bad things happen in a country precisely because most people stay silent. Asked how many of the people he's invested in would be resisters, he says he'd like to think so, but he's not sure.

points.h: The painter who gave himself only one day off a year
points.body: Frank Auerbach was a refugee from Nazi Germany, and Moritz calls him a complete monomaniac: except for one day off each Christmas to rest at Brighton Pier, he painted every single day. His models were a small fixed group of people, the same few faces painted for decades; one model who lived in Venice flew to London once a week to sit for him. His wife's house was right on the British coast, and Moritz asked if he ever went; he answered: I've never been to that house. Moritz uses this to discuss the cost of monomania—the cost to relationships is almost inevitable, but sometimes great things come out of it.

points.h: He bet on something beyond the résumé
points.body: Around 1985, Moritz was still a journalist and wrote to five small funds looking for a job. Everyone except Don Valentine said he had no technical background, no engineering degree, no experience at a tech company, and suggested he go into PR or marketing. Don was willing to take a risk, for a straightforward reason: he had seen several people with operating backgrounds at large tech companies who moved into investing and didn't succeed, and he had also seen several who did—an actuary, and the one he cited most, Arthur Rock: an investment banker by background, with nothing in his background that predicted success. Don didn't believe in teaching people; he believed in throwing them into the deep end and seeing if they drown.

points.h: Venture capital's advantage was imperfect information
points.body: Moritz says doing venture capital in the 1980s and '90s had several advantages that have now disappeared, the first being imperfect information: before the internet, unless you were close to something, you didn't know what was happening, whereas now the whole world basically gets the same information. The second is that the early market has far too many participants—individuals, two- or three-person funds, giant mutual funds—too many middlemen, and it's no longer possible for investors to build the kind of real, close relationship with founders they once had. He therefore says a moderately smart, mentally agile 14- to 16-year-old could have done venture capital in the mid-'80s; he's not sure he could do it well today.

points.h: He unabashedly believes in the great man theory
points.body: Asked whether history is shaped by great individuals or enduring institutions, Moritz's answer is blunt: he is a firm believer in the great man theory. From Lee Iacocca to Steve Jobs, from politics to the battlefield, what matters is great leaders; and of course there are also tyrants who cast a shadow over tens of millions of people for decades. Whether he was running Sequoia or writing about Ferguson, he cared about the same thing—how an organization stays alive across decades. And speaking of Elon, he says he is completely stunned by the scale of his achievements across multiple different industries, and thinks he may be the greatest industrialist in American history.

points.h: The more AI writes, the more valuable a human voice becomes
points.body: Moritz says that because AI can easily produce vast amounts of text, excellent writing that cuts through the garbage is actually appreciating in value; his definition of excellent writing is "a voice you can hear that is unmistakably the author's." The hardest thing for a writer is to get close enough to your own inner feelings and voice that it outweighs the weight of others' expectations—he quotes Joseph Campbell: the privilege of a lifetime is to become who you truly are, and that is also the hardest thing. He doesn't consider himself a technologist and says AI is rarely discussed at home; on employment he is optimistic: people predicted doomsday when the atomic bomb exploded, and in the 1970s they predicted a genetic revolution creating humans, and neither happened, so this time he thinks more jobs will be created than destroyed.
